'''Judith Aitken Ramaley''' (1941 &ndash; August 24, 2026) was an American [[biologist]] and academic administrator who served as president of several colleges and universities.<ref>
{{cite web
|url= http://www.winona.edu/president/1304.htm
|title= President Ramaley's Bio
|accessdate= 2008-05-12
|publisher= [[Winona State University]]
|archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20071122203959/http://www.winona.edu/president/1304.htm |archivedate = 2007-11-22}}
</ref> She was the president of [[Winona State University]] from 2005 to 2012.<ref name=WDN05062012>{{cite news
  |first=Nathan
  |last=Hansen  |url=http://www.winonadailynews.com/news/local/article_3b8e5ee8-9738-11e1-90ee-0019bb2963f4.html
  |title=Judith Ramaley: A legacy of growth in 7 years at WSU
  |work=[[Winona Daily News]]
  |date=May 6, 2012
  |accessdate=2012-12-04
}}</ref>
Ramaley coined the STEM acronym (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) in 2001, when she served as director of the National Science Foundation’s Education and Human Resources Division.<ref>Eleanor Chute, “STEM Education Is Branching Out,” ''Pittsburgh Post-Gazette'', February 10, 2009, https://www.post-gazette.com/news/education/2009/02/10/STEM-education-is-branching-out/stories/200902100165</ref><ref>Jerome Christenson, “Ramaley Coined STEM Term Now Used Nationwide,” ''Winona Daily News'', November 13, 2011, http://www.winonadailynews.com/news/local/article_457afe3e-0db3-11e1-abe0-001cc4c03286.html</ref>

==Biography==
Ramaley was born in 1941. She earned a bachelor's degree from [[Swarthmore College]] in 1963, a Ph.D. from the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] in 1966, and pursued postdoctoral studies at [[Indiana University]].  Ramaley began her career at the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] where she rose to assistant vice president for academic affairs. She served as the 6th president of the [[Association for Women in Science]] from 1978 to 1980.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AWIS History Association for Women in Science |url=https://awis.org/about-awis/awis-history/ |access-date=2026-08-21 |website=AWIS |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 1982, Ramaley became the chief academic officer at the [[State University of New York at Albany]], also serving as executive vice president for academic affairs.  Ramaley was the executive vice chancellor at the [[University of Kansas]] from 1987 to 1990 before stepping in as acting president at SUNY Albany. In the fall of 1990, she became the president of [[Portland State University]] until 1997<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-12-23|title=Judith Ramaley (1941-) |url=https://www.oregonencyclopedia.org/articles/ramaley-judith/ |access-date=2026-08-21 |website=www.oregonencyclopedia.org |language=en}}</ref>, and from 1997 to 2001 she served as president of the [[University of Vermont|University of Vermont.]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Former President Judith A. Ramaley (1997 - 2001) {{!}} Board... |url=https://www.uvm.edu/trustees/former-president-judith-ramaley-1997-2001 |access-date=2026-08-21 |website=www.uvm.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Ramaley resigned from the presidency of the University of Vermont after less than four years, following a hazing scandal involving the hockey team and a union drive by the faculty.<ref>{{cite web
|url= http://www2.ljworld.com/news/2001/feb/11/ramaley_resigns_vermont/
|title= Ramaley resigns Vermont post
|accessdate= 2008-06-14
|publisher= Lawrence Journal-World & News
|archive-date= 2016-03-03
|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160303202124/http://www2.ljworld.com/news/2001/feb/11/ramaley_resigns_vermont/
|url-status= dead
}}</ref>
 
Ramaley later became Assistant Director, Education and Human Resources Directorate (EHR), at the [[National Science Foundation]].
On July 18, 2005 Ramaley began her service as the 14th president of Winona State University in [[Winona, Minnesota]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Winona State University |date=2006-04-07 |title=Inauguration of Judith A. Ramaley: 14th President of Winona State University |url=https://openriver.winona.edu/presidentsvideos/2 |journal=President's Videos}}</ref>

Upon her resignation from the Winona State presidency she became a distinguished professor of public service at Portland State University.<ref name=WDN05062012 /> She died on August 24, 2026.
